prompt: Edit this text so that it is easier for its readers to understand. Keep every technical detail.
input:
When two windows saved the same note within a second, the second save could silently overwrite the first. On macOS APFS snapshots, `NoteStore.save()` checked modification times at one-second resolution, so those writes looked identical. The store now checks an `xxhash64` content hash in `note.meta.json`. If it detects a conflict, it saves the second edit as `<name>.conflict-<timestamp>.md` and shows a toast instead of overwriting the note. Windows also call `NoteStore.reconcile()` on focus.

Existing notes get a hash the first time they're opened, so there's no up-front migration. Hashing a 2 MB note takes about 3 ms. This adds 14 tests in `note_store.test.ts`, including fake-clock coverage. The Linux inotify debounce is unchanged at 250 ms and may still fire twice.

On Tuesday, 18% of checkout requests in eu-west returned HTTP 503 during a 47-minute incident. A config push raised the Postgres primary's `max_connections` from 400 to 1,200 without changing PgBouncer's `default_pool_size` of 40 per pod. During the promotion, the checkout autoscaler went from 30 to 90 pods, creating demand for 3,600 connections against PgBouncer's `max_client_conn` limit of 2,000.

A synthetic probe alerted nine minutes into the incident. The PgBouncer saturation dashboard had no alert of its own. The on-call engineer rolled back the autoscaler's maximum to 40 pods, and checkout recovered six minutes later. We'll alert when `cl_waiting` exceeds 50, set the autoscaler's maximum from a connection budget, and load-test promotional traffic.

input:
Thanks for covering the successful refresh path. Could we make concurrent 401s share one `refreshPromise` in `auth/client.ts`? Right now, three requests can all call `refreshToken()` with the same token. Once the first refresh rotates it, the others can trip reuse detection and log the user out. If callers await the same in-flight promise, they can all retry after a single refresh.

Please also limit refresh and retry to 401s. A 403 should go back to the caller as-is. One smaller fix: `expiresAt` is in seconds, but `Date.now()` returns milliseconds. Convert them to the same unit before comparing.

input:
### How CI works

GitHub Actions runs `pnpm lint`, type checking, and unit tests on every pull request. The unit tests run in four shards. Playwright end-to-end tests run only when a PR changes files under `apps/web/`. Fork PRs don't have access to secrets, so they skip staging end-to-end tests; a maintainer can request those tests by commenting `/e2e`.

The merge queue retests PRs against the latest `main` in batches of up to five. If a batch fails, the queue splits it to isolate the failure. Tests tagged `@flaky` get up to two retries and are tracked on a dashboard. Untagged tests never retry. CI caches the pnpm store and Playwright browsers using the lockfile hash.

prompt: Edit this text so that it is easier for its readers to understand. Keep every technical detail.
input:
We will evaluate feature flags from a per-tenant LRU cache held in each process, rather than from Redis. The main reason is read volume. Each node serves about 40,000 flag reads per second, and a Redis round trip adds 0.8ms at the median, while an in-process lookup takes roughly 2µs. Flags also change rarely, at a median of 3 changes per tenant per day, so the cache is almost always right and a network hop on every read buys us very little.
Invalidation uses the Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY channel `flags_changed`. Each node subscribes and evicts or refreshes the affected tenant when a notification arrives. If the connection drops, the node does a full reload on reconnect. The cost of this design is staleness: a node can serve outdated flags until it reconnects, and the worst window we have observed is 12 seconds. We judged that acceptable for flags that change this seldom. Memory is modest too. With 5,000 tenants at about 20KB each, a node holds around 100MB.
We also considered Redis with client-side caching through RESP3 tracking, which would have kept Redis as the source of truth. We rejected it because our Redis client library does not support tracking, and our managed Redis runs version 6.0, which has a known tracking bug. We should revisit this decision if the tenant count grows past 20,000, since the per-node memory footprint would then be a real concern.

Version 3.2 is out, and it is mostly about helping you concentrate on the paragraph you are writing. It also adds a line height setting, fixes an annoying paste bug, and brings native builds to Windows on ARM.
The headline feature is the new focus band, which dims every block except the one your cursor is in, so the rest of the document fades into the background while you work. Turn it on or off with Cmd+Shift+F. You can set how strongly the other blocks are dimmed anywhere from 20% to 80% opacity under Settings > Appearance. If you have reduced motion enabled on your system, the band switches without a fade animation. One known limitation: the focus band does not work in split view yet. Elsewhere in this release, the line height setting accepts values from 1.2 to 1.8, pasting from Google Docs no longer adds extra blank lines, and Windows ARM users now get a native build.

Subject: Orders database migration status

The migration of the orders service from MySQL 5.7 to Postgres 16 is on track. We have been dual-writing to both databases since Oct 3, and the backfill of 410M rows finished on Nov 18. Checksums match on 99.998% of rows. We traced the mismatches to the MySQL `utf8` charset, which is 3-byte and truncates emoji in the notes field, so the Postgres copy is the more accurate one.

Next, we will switch reads for 5% of traffic to Postgres on Dec 2 and ramp to 100% by Dec 9, as long as the error rate stays under 0.1%. Rollback is simple: reads can flip back to MySQL within a minute using the flag `orders_read_pg`. Writes will continue going to both databases until January.

We need two things from your teams. First, please freeze schema changes to the orders tables from Dec 1 through Dec 12. Second, any team that owns reporting jobs must point them at the new read replica, `orders-pg-ro`, by Dec 5. Let me know if either date is a problem for you.

prompt: Edit this text so that it is easier for its readers to understand. Keep every technical detail.
input:
This PR fixes a data race in the token refresh path where two goroutines could issue refresh requests for the same credential at the same time.
The race was in `internal/auth/manager.go:212`. Two goroutines calling `refresh()` both saw `expiresAt.Before(now)` return true, both acquired the mutex, and both sent a POST to the IdP token endpoint. The IdP then invalidated the first refresh token, so whichever response landed second got a 400, and the manager fell back to full re-auth. Under load that path added 1.8s to p99 on `/v1/tokens`, and we were hitting it roughly 14 times a minute in staging.
The fix routes refreshes through singleflight: `manager.refresh()` now calls `g.Do("refresh:"+credID, ...)` so concurrent callers wait for and share the first caller's result. The mutex around the token struct stays, but the HTTP call now happens outside it, which unblocks `Valid()` calls that were previously stuck behind a slow IdP response. I added a regression test in `manager_race_test.go` that spawns 64 goroutines against a stubbed IdP and asserts exactly one POST: it fails on `main` and passes here. `go test -race ./internal/auth/...` ran clean for 500 iterations, and the staging soak at 200 rps shows refresh calls down to ~1/min and p99 down to 210ms.

input:
From 09:32 to 10:07 UTC on 2026-09-14, `ingest-api` dropped about 31% of webhook deliveries and returned 503s for another 12% of requests.
The trigger was the 09:28 deploy of ingest-api@4.19.0. It shipped a `values.yaml` change that cut `MAX_POOL_SIZE` from 40 to 10, a staging value that had been pasted into the prod config without anyone noticing. With 10 connections serving a steady 180 rps of inserts into `events`, checkout time on the primary climbed from 6ms p50 to about 900ms, requests stacked up in `pool.Acquire()`, and the 2s request deadline started firing.
The pool saturation was on the Grafana dashboard nine minutes before the first alert: `pg_pool_waiting` crossed 40 at 09:37. The alert for that panel had its threshold left at 5 from a load test months ago, so it never paged. The SLO burn alert finally fired at 09:41, and on-call rolled back to 4.18.2 at 09:52. Deliveries were fully recovered by 10:07 as the dead-letter queue drained; no manual replay was needed because consumers retry anything with `retry_count < 5`. Two follow-ups are open: `pg_pool_waiting` now pages at 15 for 2 minutes, and `scripts/check-config-drift.sh` diffs `values.yaml` against prod defaults in CI before any release deploy. The pool-size change itself is going through a load test in the perf environment before it ships again.

prompt: Edit this text so that it is easier for its readers to understand. Keep every technical detail.
input:
For the new `feature_usage` rollup we looked at two homes: a Postgres table alongside `events`, or DuckDB files written by the nightly batch job.
Postgres needs no new infrastructure. The dashboard already has read-replica credentials, and the query would be a plain SQL join. But the rollup is a full re-aggregation by day and tenant: about 42M rows scanned per run and 2.1M rows upserted per hour. When we trialed it on the `r7g.2xlarge` primary, the upserts ran 8 minutes at a 60% CPU floor, competing directly with the ingest path we're trying to relieve, and every new dashboard query would mean another `ON CONFLICT` index on `(tenant_id, day, feature)`. We've regretted that kind of index churn before.
DuckDB keeps the rollup entirely off Postgres. The job reads from the replica, aggregates, and writes one `rollups/usage-YYYY-MM-DD.duckdb` file per day to object storage; the dashboard service opens whichever day files it needs with zero contention against ingest. The same 42M-row scan ran in 11 seconds in the trial. The cost is a small reader we'd own, about 90 lines in `internal/rollups/read.go` plus per-file schema checks, and losing ad-hoc SQL joins across days, which nothing in the dashboard spec needs. Since the dashboard is the only consumer and it tolerates 5-minute staleness, we're going with DuckDB, keeping the Postgres path behind `ROLLUPS_BACKEND=pg` for one release as a rollback.

prompt: Edit this text so that it is easier for its readers to understand. Keep every technical detail.
input:
What you're seeing is that default arguments are evaluated once, at `def` time, not on every call. So `def add_tag(tag, tags=[])` doesn't give each call a fresh list: every call that omits `tags` shares the one list created when the module was imported. You can watch it happen, `add_tag.__defaults__` is `([],)`, and it's the same list object across calls. That's why your tags accumulate across requests, and why it only bites when a call skips the argument, since passing `tags=[]` explicitly builds a new list each time.
The fix is the `None` sentinel: `def add_tag(tag, tags=None)`, then `tags = [] if tags is None else tags` inside the body. Use `is None` rather than `== None`, because `==` dispatches to `__eq__` and a hostile `tags` value can lie about equality. If you're in a dataclass, the same rule shows up as `field(default_factory=list)`; the old spelling `tags: list = []` raises a `ValueError` at class creation for exactly this reason.
It's worth knowing why the language works this way. Defaults live in a tuple on the function object, which lets the interpreter skip argument parsing for omitted args and lets C extensions bind them cheaply. It has never been changed because per-call evaluation would break code that deliberately shares the default as a cache, and the stdlib relies on that in a handful of places, mostly around compiled-pattern wrappers.
must_preserve: tags = [] if tags is None else tags

prompt: Edit this text so that it is easier for its readers to understand. Keep every technical detail.
input:
v3 makes the core read API asynchronous: `fetchAll()` now returns `Promise<Row[]>`, and there is no synchronous equivalent. Every call site that uses the result needs an `await`, and the enclosing function needs `async`, or you will silently pass a promise around where rows used to be. That was the single most common break in the 47 call sites we migrated in our own app.
The mechanical part is small: search for `fetchAll(` and add `await` where the result is used directly, e.g. `const rows = await fetchAll(sql)`. The sites that need thought are the ones passing the result straight into another call, like `parse(fetchAll(sql))`, which becomes `parse(await fetchAll(sql))`. Error handling changes shape too: instead of `try/catch` around a returned null, failures now surface as promise rejections. If you had `if (!rows)` guarding a failed query, that branch is dead in v3, because failures throw and `rows` is always a fully populated array on success.
Two smaller breaks in the same release: the callback form `fetchAll(sql, cb)` is gone (drop the callback and use `await`), and `Row` is now generic, so typed queries look like `fetchAll<UserRow>(sql)` while untyped calls still compile. Run `npx ourlib codemod v3` before touching anything by hand. In our trial it rewrote 39 of 47 call sites automatically and logged the remaining 8 with reasons, mostly `await` inside a non-async callback passed to `map`.

Team status for the week of Nov 16. The `checkout-v2` migration is done ahead of schedule: we cut the last two holdout endpoints (`/api/cart/apply-coupon`, `/api/cart/tax`) over to v2 on Wednesday, so 100% of cart traffic now hits the new service. p99 checkout latency is holding at 240ms versus 380ms before the cutover, and error rate is flat at 0.4%. The remaining wart is that `apply-coupon` still makes a synchronous call to the legacy promotions service; the 60s cache going in next week should drop that from ~7% of requests to under 1%.
Alert noise is fixed. On-call was absorbing 40+ pages a day from the `redis-memory` alert flapping on the session store; Doris moved the threshold from 78% to 85% and added a 5-minute for-window, and we've been at roughly 3 pages a day for the last four days. Real detection didn't suffer. Both genuine incidents this week, including a 12-minute API blip from a bad deploy that was rolled back, were caught by the same alerts as before the change.
One risk to flag for next weekend: the nightly search reindex needs a 90-minute window on the `elasticsearch` cluster while we re-shard from 12 to 24 shards, scheduled Saturday 02:00 UTC. Search results will be up to 10 minutes stale during the re-shard. Nothing customer-facing should notice, but I'll post in #eng if the window slips so nobody burns time chasing ghost search bugs.
